lesson.title: O(n): Linear Time and the Cost of Looking at Everything
lesson.summary: An algorithm runs in linear time, O(n), when the amount of work it performs grows in direct proportion to the size of its input, typically because it touches each input element roughly once.
lesson.body:
Linear time, O(n), is what you get whenever an algorithm has to look at every element of its input at least once, doing a constant amount of work per element. If the input doubles, the work roughly doubles. If the input grows tenfold, the work grows roughly tenfold. This proportional relationship is what makes the growth linear, a straight line if you were to graph running time against input size.

A single unnested loop over the input is the classic signature of O(n) code.

def sum_all(values):
    total = 0
    for v in values:
        total += v
    return total

This function performs one addition per element, so for a list of n numbers it performs n additions, and its time complexity is O(n). The same is true of searching for a value in an unsorted list, finding the maximum value in a list, or counting how many elements satisfy some condition. All of these need to inspect every element at least once in the worst case, because skipping any single element risks missing the answer.

Let's connect this to counting operations directly. In sum_all, the loop body, total += v, runs exactly n times for a list of length n. There is also a small constant amount of setup work, total = 0, and a return statement, but those happen once regardless of n. So the total operation count is roughly n + 2. When we apply Big-O, we drop the constant term because it becomes insignificant next to n once n is large, leaving O(n).

The doubling thought experiment is especially clean for linear time. Suppose sum_all takes 2 milliseconds to sum a list of 1 million numbers. Because it is O(n), doubling the list to 2 million numbers should take roughly 4 milliseconds, and doubling again to 4 million numbers should take roughly 8 milliseconds. The time grows in lockstep with the input, which is exactly what linear means.

Linear time sits in the middle of the growth rates you will meet in this unit. It is slower than O(1) and O(log n), which barely react to input size at all, but it is dramatically faster than O(n^2), where work grows much faster than the input does. Recognizing a single pass over the data, one loop, no nesting, doing a fixed amount of work per element, is one of the most useful skills you can build for reading code and predicting its performance at a glance.
